It is essential to offer prisoners both theoretical and practical education, enabling them to reintegrate into society effectively. The primary goal of penal institutions should not be to humiliate or degrade individuals, as this can foster resentment and further criminal behavior. Prisoners' conventional striped uniforms ought to be substituted with more respectful clothing that continues to denote their status as inmates. This change can help reduce the stigma associated with incarceration and make it easier for ex-convicts to find employment upon release. The implementation of the Bertillon or French method for measuring and registering prisoners can guarantee clear identification of inmates without requiring noticeable attire. One of the significant challenges in prison reform is the reintegration of ex-convicts into society after serving long sentences. The awareness of their prior criminal record and the fact that others are aware of their time in prison may result in obstacles regarding employment and gaining trust. This can lead to feelings of alienation and a sense of being an outcast, potentially pushing them back towards criminal activities. To tackle this problem, prison-related groups have been established to aid former inmates after their release, offering them direction and help in securing jobs and furthering their rehabilitation. These organizations, made up of philanthropists and businesspeople, can assist in bridging the divide between the prison and society, providing hope and an opportunity for a new beginning. The furlough program implemented at the Elmira Reformatory offers a distinctive method for helping former prisoners reintegrate into society. Under this system, inmates are granted a three-year furlough, during which they are subjected to beneficial influences and provided with chances to further their rehabilitation beyond the prison environment. They must report to the prison authorities on a monthly basis, and if they show adequate advancement and hold positions of trust, they are awarded a final release, indicating their capacity to act as accountable citizens. A reform school in Kansas, akin to the Elmira system, should be established to meet the requirements of juvenile offenders and keep them apart from experienced criminals. Although such institutions can be expensive, it is crucial to recognize the value of investing in the rehabilitation of individuals who have committed crimes. A well-managed reformatory could potentially support itself while providing effective rehabilitation for its inmates. The Kansas Legislature has recently allocated funds to complete the Hutchinson Reformatory, which will help alleviate the overcrowding in existing penitentiaries and cater to a demographic that is currently underserved. Discharged prisoners from other institutions, such as Lansing, often find employment in mines or other trades, with the prison authorities offering general assistance in job placement. While this discussion has addressed different facets of criminology and penology in Kansas, a more scientific examination of the topic is set to take place alongside the study of sociology at the University of Kansas. Additionally, Frank H. Hodder's concise bibliography on municipal government in the United States emphasizes the necessity for further in-depth research on subjects that significantly affect citizens' lives, including taxation and municipal governance.

In the field of ethics, a major issue emerges when moral judgment is based on personal wants, since not all individuals naturally have a wish to act morally. This situation can lead to conflicts where an individual may justify their immoral actions by claiming a lack of desire for morality. One way to tackle this issue is to clearly differentiate between rationality and morality. Rationality, when assessed from the standpoint of an agent's personal beliefs and desires, could regard immoral actions as rational if the agent does not possess moral desires. Thus, such actions may be considered rationally justifiable, even though they remain immoral. However, the presence of a distinction between reason and ethics continues to be a subject of debate. Metaethics, as a philosophical discipline, holds significant importance in Hume's perspective regarding this issue. At the core of his view lies the is-ought distinction, which asserts a basic separation between statements describing facts and those prescribing moral or evaluative claims. Is-statements pertain to factual information about the natural world, while ought-statements encompass moral or evaluative assertions about what ought to be done or what holds value. The core of this difference is that is-statements do not necessarily lead to ought-statements by themselves. Hume underscores this idea, as he holds that mixing these kinds of statements has traditionally been a frequent cause of mistakes in philosophical thinking. Drawing from this distinction, various related philosophical theories have been attributed to Hume in relation to ongoing metaethical debates. One such debate revolves around the conflict between cognitivism and non-cognitivism. Cognitivists assert that moral judgments possess objective truth values, while non-cognitivists claim that moral statements do not convey factual content but instead express feelings, inclinations, or imperatives. This ongoing discourse highlights the complexity and depth of metaethical inquiry, reflecting the diverse perspectives on the nature of moral language and reasoning.

1000-Word Philosophy is an online anthology that features concise essays on a variety of philosophical subjects. Each entry is restricted to 1000 words, offering an easy-to-read and manageable structure for those exploring philosophical topics. The anthology was founded in 2014 by Andrew D. Chapman, a philosophy lecturer at the University of Colorado, Boulder. In 2018, Nathan Nobis, a philosophy professor at Morehouse College, assumed the position of editor-in-chief. Initially, the anthology primarily featured works by graduates of the University of Colorado at Boulder's Ph.D. program in philosophy. However, the scope has since expanded, and contributors now hail from around the world. The essays in 1000-Word Philosophy aim to present intricate philosophical subjects in a straightforward and succinct way. They often include references or sources for further exploration of the subject matter. This collection functions as an essential tool for individuals looking to engage with philosophical topics in a more accessible manner. For those interested in following 1000-Word Philosophy, it has a presence on various social media platforms, including Facebook and Twitter. Readers might also delve into related philosophical conversations on The Stone, a philosophy blog. References and external links offer additional avenues for readers to interact with the material and delve deeper into the realm of philosophy.

The Princess found herself in a precarious situation, torn between the allure of the Duc de Guise and the fear of the torment a jealous husband might inflict. Her contemplations led her to make new resolutions, yet these were quickly forgotten upon the sight of the Duc. The recent partnership between their families created many chances for the Duc to spend time with her, and he carefully detailed every conversation he had with Madame. Despite his attempts to suppress the jealousy caused by Madame's beauty, it was only through many promises that he succeeded in giving her some comfort. This very jealousy, however, enabled the Princess to protect the remaining portion of her heart from the Duc's pursuits, despite the fact that he had already gained a considerable share of her affection. The union of the King with the Emperor Maximilian's daughter introduced a sense of merriment and festivity into the court. The King organized a ballet featuring Madame and the princesses, with the Princess de Montpensier standing out as a rival to Madame in terms of beauty. The Duc d'Anjou and four other individuals were scheduled to portray Moors, wearing matching costumes as was traditional for this type of performance. Before the ballet commenced and he donned his mask, the Duc de Guise whispered a few words to the Princess as he passed by, an act that did not go unnoticed by her husband, the Prince, causing her great unease. Later, seeing the Duc d'Anjou in his masked attire, she mistook him for the Duc de Guise and implored him, "Do not bestow your gaze upon anyone but Madame tonight; I shall not be the least bit jealous. "I command you to keep your distance from me," she declared, and with that, she swiftly withdrew, leaving the Duc d'Anjou astonished. He recognized that he faced a powerful adversary, and the mention of Madame clearly pointed to the Duc de Guise, showing that his sister was not the preferred choice compared to the Princess de Montpensier. This realization, along with jealousy, frustration, and anger, intensified his wrath. Without his natural talent for concealing his feelings, he would have immediately attacked the Duc de Guise at that moment. However, he did not hold back from disclosing his awareness of the secret matter. As they exited the salon, the Duc d'Anjou confronted the Duc de Guise, saying, "It is too much to presume to look upon my sister and to steal the affection of the woman I love." The King's presence prevents me from acting now, but remember that the loss of your life may be the least of your punishments for your impertinence." The Duc de Guise, not accustomed to such threats, was unable to respond immediately due to the King's summons. Yet, he did not forget the slight and sought revenge throughout his life. From that evening on, the Duc d'Anjou worked to make the King turn against the Duc de Guise. He convinced the King that Madame would never agree to her proposed marriage to the King of Navarre as long as the Duc de Guise was allowed to maintain contact with her. He argued that it was unacceptable for a subject to obstruct a union that could bring peace to France for his own vanity. The King, who already had a prejudice against the Duc de Guise, became even more enraged by these remarks. The next day, when the Duc presented himself to join the ball at the Queen's apartments, the King brusquely questioned his intentions, rejecting his services and turning away without further acknowledgment. Undeterred, the Duc de Guise entered the room, incensed against both the King and the Duc d'Anjou. His arrogance caused him to focus even more on Madame, whereas the remarks of the Duc d'Anjou kept him from turning his gaze toward the Princess de Montpensier. The Duc d'Anjou observed them closely, noticing the Princess's chagrin when the Duc de Guise spoke with Madame. Realizing her jealousy, he hoped to sow discord and approached her, saying, "It is in your interest that I tell you the Duc de Guise does not deserve your preference over me. He is misleading and disloyal to you concerning my sister, just as he previously disloyal to her regarding you. He is driven by ambition, but since he pleases you, I shall not stand in the way of your happiness. It would be undignified to pursue a heart already taken. I have only attracted your indifference, and I would not wish to replace it with dislike." Overcome with love and sadness, the Duc d'Anjou could barely finish his speech. Initially motivated by spite and vengeance, he was deeply affected by the thought of losing the Princess's beauty and affection. Without waiting for her response, he left the ball, claiming illness, and returned home to nurse his sorrows. The Princess de Montpensier remained, understandably distressed and anxious.

The protagonist, having returned from a long absence, finds himself unknown to his family and friends, as no news of his return had reached them in the twelve months since his departure. After a brief period, he explains the reasons for his visit and, upon settling his affairs, contemplates a return to New York. His brother suggests a gathering of their siblings the following morning to explore alternative solutions. They advise him to stay in safety, believing that no one would trouble him if he were to remain at home, and recommend that he make his presence known in the neighborhood where he is well-known, while avoiding the towns. They predict that after a few days, he would no longer draw attention. Heeding their advice, he visits the King's Cove and is astonished to find that even those who knew him do not recognize him until they hear his voice. On the Sabbath, he attends a service at Trevean, where he experiences a profound spiritual awakening. The congregation, particularly the Methodists, are overjoyed to see him, having heard of his transformation. This surprising return to his native land overwhelms him with wonder and appreciation for God's compassion. As he participates in the preaching and meetings, he is initially reluctant to lead a hymn or pray aloud, having not done so before his return. However, after overcoming a period of intense inner turmoil, he embraces his new role with trepidation and begins to share his spiritual journey with others. His community expands quickly, and prayer gatherings emerge in different places. Within eight or nine weeks, many people come to faith, and their assemblies feature a combination of prayer, song, weeping, and worship. During a particularly memorable prayer meeting, he feels as if he is in the presence of the divine, much like his experiences in New York. Despite some initial resistance from older members, many others support his newfound calling. He emphasizes the importance of sharing one's thoughts with those who truly understand the ways of God, rather than those who may not comprehend the spiritual journey. As his spiritual journey continues, he moves through the rural areas, communicating with individuals in an easy-to-understand and approachable way. He shares a story about being invited to give a speech at a chapel that was eight or nine miles away from his home, and when he arrived, he was confused for Captain Harry Carter. Despite his initial fear and uncertainty, he moves forward to speak to the full chapel, relying on his own life experiences instead of referencing a particular scripture. Despite the growing support for his ministry, he continues to grapple with self-doubt and the fear of being called to a task he may not be ready for. He acknowledges the immense burden of his calling and the physical and emotional toll it takes on him. However, he remains steadfast in his commitment to spreading the word of God. In February 1791, or just prior, the enthusiasm of the Trevean society starts to decline, yet the gatherings continue to be favored by divine blessing. In late March or early April, he is summoned by a prominent individual from the neighborhood who expresses concern over potential trouble brewing against him. The man recounts a conversation he overheard in Helston, where some gentlemen were questioning why he, a Methodist preacher, was allowed to preach so openly without legal repercussions. Fearing for his safety, the man advises him to return to America to avoid potential legal troubles and imprisonment. He offers to provide a letter of recommendation from a nobleman, which he believes could be beneficial for him. The man, who is well-acquainted with his family, accompanies him part of the way home, leaving him to contemplate his next steps.

George Santayana was an influential American philosopher and poet, though he chose not to become an American citizen. He lived a considerable part of his life in Fascist Italy and experienced intellectual and artistic solace at Oxford University. Despite being an atheist, Santayana identified as an "aesthetic Catholic," and his final years were spent in Rome under the care of Catholic nuns. In 1941, Santayana relocated to a hospital and convent run by the Little Company of Mary, commonly referred to as the Blue Nuns, situated at 6 Via Santo Stefano Rotondo on the Celian Hill in Rome. He stayed at that place until his passing in September 1952. Santayana's desire to avoid burial in consecrated ground posed a challenge in Italy. Eventually, the Spanish consulate in Rome consented to his interment in the Pantheon of the Obra Pía Española, located within the Campo Verano cemetery in Rome. Santayana's body of philosophical writing is broad and features a number of significant publications. Among these are "The Sense of Beauty" (1896), regarded as one of the earliest major works on aesthetics published in the United States and his initial book-length monograph. "The Life of Reason" (5 volumes, 1905–06) represents the pinnacle of his academic career at Harvard. Other significant works include "Scepticism and Animal Faith" (1923) and "The Realms of Being" (4 volumes, 1927–1940). Although Santayana did not align himself with the pragmatist movement, which included figures such as William James, Charles Sanders Peirce, Josiah Royce, and John Dewey, "The Life of Reason" is often regarded as an early and comprehensive exploration of pragmatist thought. Similar to other classical pragmatists, Santayana's writings emphasize practical applications and the influence of human experience on the formation of knowledge and comprehension.

Significant advancements occurred in music and literature during the rule of King Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar (1673–1704). King Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar, also recognized by the title Sahitya Vidyanikasha Prastharam, which translates to "Expert in literature," is credited with creating "on music." His composition drew inspiration from Jayadeva's Sanskrit work "Geetha Govinda" and was composed in the saptapadi meter. This composition is renowned as the initial work to spread the Vaishnava faith through the Kannada language. During this period, Sarvajna, a mendicant and Veerashaiva poet, also made a significant impact on the Kannada-speaking region. His didactic Vachanas, written in the tripadi metre, are celebrated as some of the most important works in Kannada literature. Sarvajna's works, with few exceptions, focus on his spiritual journey as a wanderer. His brief Vachanas provide understanding of the craft of living, the significance of existence, and the manners of society. Unlike many authors of his time, Sarvajna did not seek patronage from royalty nor did he write for fame. His primary goal was to impart moral lessons to the people. Another notable figure from this era was the Brahmin author Lakshmisa, also known as Lakshmisha. A renowned storyteller and dramatist, his works date back to the mid-16th or late 17th century. "Jaimini Bharata," his version of the epic Mahabharata, is composed in the shatpadi meter and is regarded as one of the most widely appreciated poems of the late medieval era. This compilation of narratives features the story of "Sita Parityaga," or "Repudiation of Sita." The writer effectively reinterpreted a religious account as a profoundly human tale, which still appeals to people in contemporary society. The later medieval period also saw progress in different areas of music and literature, showcasing the vibrant cultural legacy of that time.

Philosophical concepts about death frequently portray it as a fundamental negative force, capable of eliminating the core nature of the world, which is viewed as the aggregate of every individual. This viewpoint suggests that non-existence exceeds existence, leading to the perception of death as providing a major and final advantage. This benefit entails everlasting peace and serenity, a notion termed "redemption" by certain philosophers, derived from the Christian vocabulary. In the context of Christianity, particularly its mystical form, the religion is interpreted as one of renunciation and salvation, which some philosophers view as a precursor to their own philosophical systems. One such philosopher is Philipp Mainländer, who emphasized the importance of ontological pluralism. According to this view, reality is defined by the existence of individual wills, each self-sufficient in terms of knowledge and ontology. Mainländer rejected Schopenhauer's metaphysical viewpoint, which claimed a cosmic universal will that surpasses individual wills. Instead, he promoted an immanent, empirical, and representational approach to knowledge, limited to the domain of individual consciousness. In this perspective, every will is fundamentally distinct from the rest, while the natural sciences demonstrate a consistent relationship between all entities in the world, with each relying on others through essential laws. This perceived discrepancy between philosophical and scientific viewpoints regarding the nature of existence and interdependence remains an active topic of discussion and inquiry within the discipline of philosophy.

The intricate woodwork of a pew in the church, which was once an eyesore, has fortunately been removed. The interior masonry exhibits a robust character, which was significantly altered when the church was covered with thick layers of plaster. During the restoration of a squint, we discovered three unique circular stones, each featuring an ornamental volute at the end. These stones, composed of oolite, are thought to have been components of a scroll located at the upper portion of a Roman (pagan) altar. One of the fragments even had remnants of salmon-colored mortar attached to it. It is worth noting an opening in the church of St. Mary, located in Dover Castle, which is in a similar position. However, it is commonly believed to be a lychnoscope, used by soldiers in the guard-room to observe the light burning at the altar on the south-east of the nave, which was specifically reserved for them. There is considerable debate regarding the correct terminology for these openings. Squints, which are typically found inside the church, should not be confused with low side-windows or lychnoscopes, which are originally unglazed and located outside. Squints primarily serve the purpose of allowing individuals in the aisles to view the elevation of the Host at the high altar. They may occasionally be linked to a side-chapel, a parvise, or a tower-chamber. Their typical height measures around 4 feet above the ground, rising to between 2 and 10 feet in total. Starting narrow, they progressively broadened and widened, as observed in St. Clement's and St. Peter's churches in Sandwich. Sometimes, when placed close to a side-altar, they functioned as a credence or featured a piscina integrated within them (as exemplified by Crawley Church in Hampshire). It is also conceivable that the sole authentic squint or hagioscope at St. Martin's Church was located behind the current piscina. The remaining openings could have served as lepers' windows or for penitents. The tower, added in the 14th century, is somewhat squat and topped with a pyramidal structure. It measures 16 feet by 13 feet 3 inches in length and width, with two large buttresses on the west side, each projecting 4 feet 3 inches. The tower is primarily constructed of flint with a slight mix of thin medieval tiles and features three louvre windows. One of these windows, with the distinctive "long and short" characteristics of Saxon stonework, may have been relocated from another part of the church. The construction of this tower likely resulted in the loss of some fascinating features at the west end of the original church. It might have served as a western apse (a feature common in early basilicas), a baptistery, or a room featuring an arch on every side. At this time, it continues to be a subject of speculation, though additional investigations could shed light on the enigma. It is wise to refrain from dogmatic assertions when one's definitive theories could be disproven at any moment. The climb up to St. Martin's Church from the lych-gate is notably impressive. After making a sharp turn on the churchyard path, one ascends nine steps to arrive at the Western Door. From this door, there is an additional ascent of eleven steps leading to the altar. This feature is reminiscent of Canterbury Cathedral. On the south wall of the tower-porch, a controversial monumental stone is embedded. Initially described as a piece of a Roman coffin, this assertion is incorrect. The inscription's character and the chamfering of the upper part, similar to the tomb of Stephen Langton in St. Michael's Chapel in the Cathedral, indicate that it dates back to the 13th century. The inscription is broken and somewhat blurred, yet one can still make out [dagger] [iota] [reverse solidus], and on the reverse side [reverse epsilon] ARISCVS. It has been suggested that this word might have been "Mariscus," implying that the stone could have been a boundary-stone of a marsh. It is more probable that it is an ordinary sepulchral slab. Until two years ago, church visitors frequently encountered disappointment. Despite being told that St. Martin's was the oldest church in England, the signs of antiquity were not immediately apparent. The Early English chancel arch was the most prominent feature, and the walls of the nave were covered with a thick layer of modern-looking yellowish plaster. It is sometimes amusing to observe the comments and behavior of casual visitors, many of whom are from the United States of America, where the church is included in the "list of sights" to be seen during their European tour. Some of the less informed visitors would briefly enter the building, make a cursory observation, and then leave with a sense of accomplishment, believing they had "done" St. Martin's.

Islamic philosophy has historically placed a significant emphasis on logic. The development of Sharia, or Islamic law, necessitated the establishment of rigorous standards for argumentation, leading to the emergence of a unique approach to logic within the discipline of Kalam. However, this initial approach was ultimately eclipsed by the impact of Greek and Hellenistic philosophy, especially through the prominence of the Mu'tazili philosophers, who held great admiration for Aristotle's Organon. The contributions of Hellenistic-influenced Islamic philosophers were instrumental in the transmission of Aristotelian logic to medieval Europe. Averroes' commentaries on the Organon, along with the writings of al-Farabi, Avicenna, and al-Ghazali, and other thinkers, were crucial in influencing the evolution of European logic during the Renaissance. These Muslim scholars frequently examined and improved upon Aristotelian logic, while simultaneously developing their own original logical systems in the process. As outlined in the Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Islamic philosophers regarded logic as a broad discipline that included not merely the examination of formal structures of reasoning and their correctness, but also aspects of the philosophy of language, epistemology, and metaphysics. Their engagement with exploring the connection between logic and language was driven by persistent disagreements with Arabic grammarians. This resulted in detailed conversations regarding the content and goals of logic in connection with reasoning and communication. In the field of formal logical analysis, Islamic philosophers developed further the theories concerning terms, propositions, and syllogisms, relying on the groundwork established by earlier thinkers and adding to the extensive body of logical thought that has influenced philosophical discussion throughout different cultures and time periods.

The public was initially unaware of the man who was both a study enthusiast and a retiree, preferring to keep his friendships limited and not seeking new ones. However, when a woman insisted on his company, he found it difficult to refuse her charm. He visited her home and was impressed by the verses of a certain abbé, which had already gained the admiration of all of Paris. However, he never got the opportunity to meet the brother of his hostess. Eventually, on a single evening during his visit to Madame de Miron, the brother arrived. She presented him and urged the visitor to read aloud some lines from a poem that had captured her attention toward him. Initially, the brother showed the same indifference as his sister, but as the recitation continued, his interest grew. He wished to invite the visitor for supper with Madame le Comtesse de Mir, but the visitor declined, not wanting to appear frivolous or easily swayed. The following morning, the brother visited the visitor, extending an invitation from Madame le Comtesse de Mir. That evening, he came to collect the visitor, and two days later, he invited the visitor to his home, introducing him to his father, his sister, and his young son. The visitor was struck by the brother's simplicity in his domestic life, contrasting with his brilliance in social settings. It soon became clear that he was a devoted son, brother, master, and father, as evidenced by his tenderness towards his young child. The two men quickly developed a mutual respect, grounded in their shared principles, despite their different exteriors. They found common ground in their love for literature, theatre, and the arts, and their indulgence towards human weaknesses. Their friendship deepened through their shared interests and the compatibility of their personalities. Their evenings were spent discussing poetry, music, and scientific discoveries, with the brother effortlessly blending wit, charm, and a generous heart. He was recognized for praising others' strengths, supporting those whose abilities were overlooked, and refraining from spreading rumors. He considered himself an advocate for the absent, and he strove to focus on the positive aspects of life. Despite the brother's financial struggles, he composed a comic opera, incorporating Spanish and Italian melodies he had brought back from Madrid. When the piece was initially rejected by the theatre of Souz, the visitor and others encouraged him to present it to the Théâtre-Français, where it would likely find success. The complex character of Beaumarchais made him a challenging figure to understand. Even amidst financial difficulties, he managed to create an enduring dramatic work. Despite the challenges he faced, he took on one of the nation's greatest injustices, emerging victorious and celebrated by the people of France. In 1772, two years prior to the legal action initiated by the Comte de la Blache against Beaumarchais, the old parliaments of the kingdom were disbanded through an unwarranted decree issued by Chancellor Maupeou, with the approval of King Louis XV. In their place, a new parliament, known as the Parliament Maupeou, was established. From the beginning, it encountered significant resistance. The country had previously honored the authority of Louis XIV, yet during Louis XV's reign, there was broad opposition to unchecked power. Although flawed, the parliaments were regarded as the sole check against the arbitrary rule of a reckless sovereign, and they earned public support every time they defied the royal decree. The parliaments became more powerful, asserting their role as a vital component of the monarchy, a representation of the nation, and the protectors of its freedom, concerns, and privileges. Each of their conflicts with the monarchy ended in victory, until Chancellor Maupeou, a man from their ranks, decided to challenge them. With the support of Madame du Barry, who held considerable sway over the King, Maupeou enacted an edict on December 7th, 1770, which significantly altered the structure of the parliaments. The Parliament of Paris opposed and refused to accept the edict, leading the Chancellor to implement exceptional actions.

The craftsmanship of Wély is genuinely enchanting, particularly in the subtle reveal of the _décolleté_, which is almost unparalleled. His draughtsmanship, a trait commonly honed within the Parisian Schools of Art, stands as a reflection of his lasting expertise, brimming with lively spirit and cleverness. Wély's work can be best described as charming, and it is worth noting that the more liberated one's tastes, the more of Wély's drawings one can appreciate in a collection. His focus is on the adventures of the bedroom, with a humorous touch rather than caricature, as he holds a deep appreciation for human beauty. Wély's style may have been influenced by Jules Chéret, the renowned poster artist. His work, similar to many contemporary illustrators, is mainly created using chalk or charcoal, a change primarily resulting from improvements in photo-reproduction techniques and the wish to imitate the stone-like drawings of earlier times by artists such as Gavarni, Daumier, and Cham. However, the elegance of pen-and-ink work has not been completely overshadowed, thanks to artists like Guillaume, Caran-d’Ache, and Job, who continue to favor this medium. Wély's delicate yet assured application of crayon, charcoal, or lithographic chalk distinguishes him. He captures the essence of his subjects with a light-hearted touch, reminiscent of Steinlen in the realm of ladies' dressing rooms or a bolder Helleu. His work often features the artist-model relationship and the carefree, struggling artists, depicted with a delightful sense of humor. In one of his infrequent pen and ink works displayed in _Cocorico_, a stylish woman in a store humorously interacts with a shop assistant, while another illustration portrays two Parisian women conversing on a pier. Wély's method is apparent through the quick, strong lines that define the figures, with shading and color applied using skillful crayon strokes. His enjoyment in manipulating his medium is palpable, as seen in the precise modeling of delicate features with just the right touch of chalk. Wély's work in publications such as _Frou Frou_ and _La Vie en Rose_ showcases talent, wit, and energy. His illustrations for "Aristophane à Paris" and "La Maîtresse du Prince Jean" are notable for their skill and lively spirit. A particular drawing, _Quelques Predictions pour 1902_, brings to life a coquette in déshabillé consulting a fortune-teller, with a kitten playing nearby, so vividly that they seem ready to move off the page. Louis Malteste is another exceptional artist whose work is characterized by a steady flow of conscientious and sound pieces. His draftsmanship is unerring, and he excels at capturing individual character without resorting to eccentricity or sensationalism. Malteste's work was particularly notable during the Dreyfus trials, where he produced spirited and life-like sketches under challenging conditions. His talent has been recognized by publishers and illustrated papers such as _Le Monde Illustré_ and _L’Illustration_, and his more fanciful subjects have found a home in publications like _La Vie en Rose_, _Le Rire_, and _L’Assiette au Beurre_. Malteste's drawings in _La Vie en Rose_ are particularly striking, often executed in chalk and capturing actions driven by sudden impulse. His style, similar to that of the English draftsman Gunning King, is probably shaped by the experienced Renouard. Malteste's creations are rich in personality, exemplified by his series of coachmen and his colored portraits of rulers. His tender colorist touch is evident in a milking scene entitled _La Traité des Blanches_, and his black and white work, such as _Le Fléau_, is equally impressive. His exploration of distinctive human figures, including _Femmes Fidèles_, _La Femme qui prise_, and _Woman with a Dog_, stands out for their lifelike portrayals and the unique characters they express. His skill in conveying the essence of his subjects through exceptional drawing is a notable feature of Malteste's work.

The Church of God and Saints of Christ is a religious organization that traces its origins to the United States. It is known for its unique blend of Jewish and Christian practices, which has contributed to its distinctive identity. The church is considered one of the oldest African-American congregations in the United States that adheres to the tenets of Judaism. From 2001 until his death in 2016, the church was led by Rabbi Jehu A. Crowdy, Jr., a great-grandson of the founder, William Saunders Crowdy. Since 2016, Phillip E. McNeil has been at the helm of the organization. As of 2005, the church had established fifty tabernacles across the United States, with many more in Africa, reflecting its growing influence and reach. The Church of God and Saints of Christ holds a unique perspective on religious history, teaching that all Jews were originally black and that African Americans are descendants of the lost tribes of Israel. This doctrine is fundamental to the church's identity and shapes its methodology in religious observance. Members of the church believe that Jesus was neither God nor the son of God, but rather an adherent of Judaism and a prophet. This perspective sets the church apart from mainstream Christian beliefs and underscores its commitment to a distinct interpretation of religious texts and traditions. The Church of God and Saints of Christ highly respects its founder, William Saunders Crowdy, viewing him as a prophet. This reverence for the founder is an integral part of the church's religious practices and beliefs. In terms of rituals, the Church of God and Saints of Christ combines aspects from both Judaism and Christianity. They have adopted rites from both the Old and New Testaments, creating a unique blend of religious practices. Old Testament observances include the use of the Jewish calendar, the celebration of Passover, the circumcision of infant males, the commemoration of the Sabbath on Saturday, and the wearing of yarmulkes. New Testament practices encompass baptism through immersion and footwashing, both of which trace their roots to Old Testament traditions. The Commandment Keepers Congregation, another religious organization, was founded by Wentworth Arthur Matthew in Harlem in 1919. Matthew was influenced by non-black Jews, as well as by Marcus Garvey and the Universal Negro Improvement Association and African Communities League. This organization serves as another illustration of the varied religious environment in the United States, where each group presents its distinct understanding of religious scriptures and customs.

"Arnold had been expecting this man, yet here he was, detained as a spy! Had the letters simply been distractions? It was a mystery Arnold could not solve. However, the instructions from his General were clear, and without delay, he sent the man to Headquarters. Major Benjamin Tallmadge, through two letters to Jared Sparks, recounts events from September 23rd to the 24th. He describes the profound impact on him of the incidents involving Arnold, the traitor, and Major André, the victim. The 2nd Regiment of Light Dragoons, under Colonel Sheldon, was stationed near North Castle, with Lieutenant Colonel Jameson in command in Sheldon's absence. On the morning of September 23rd, 1780, Tallmadge led a detachment of Dragoons to scout the area below the White Plains to East Chester, a neutral zone. Returning late that evening, he learned of a prisoner named John Anderson. Upon investigation, he discovered that three men—John Paulding, David Williams, and Isaac Van Wart—had encountered Anderson en route to New York. Finding hidden papers in Anderson's boots, they decided to detain him and bring him to the Regiment's headquarters near North Castle, where he was handed over to Lieutenant Colonel Jameson. At the time, General Washington was scheduled to meet with the French Commander, Count Rochambeau, at Hartford, Connecticut, and was returning to the Army when Anderson was captured. Upon reaching Jameson's quarters on the evening of the 23rd, Tallmadge was astonished to learn that Anderson had been sent to Arnold's Headquarters at West Point with a letter detailing his capture. Simultaneously, an express was dispatched with the discovered papers to meet General Washington, who was on his way back to West Point. Tallmadge was surprised by this approach and conveyed his worries to Jameson in private. The Lieutenant Colonel showed signs of unease, particularly when Tallmadge suggested a strategy he was prepared to fully commit to, though he refrained from elaborating more. Unable to persuade Jameson, Tallmadge devised a plan to bring the prisoner back to their quarters, which he managed to achieve, albeit with reluctance from Jameson. As the order was about to be sent, Jameson insisted on sending his letter to General Arnold, which turned out to be the first indication the traitor received that his scheme had been uncovered. The officer returned with his prisoner early the next morning. They decided it was safest to take the prisoner to Salem, to Colonel Sheldon's quarters, with Tallmadge appointed to oversee him. Upon reaching Salem, the prisoner's anxiety increased, and later that afternoon, he asked for pen, ink, and paper. He composed a letter addressed to General Washington, dated 'Salem, 24th September, 1780,' identifying himself as Major John André, Adjutant General of the British Army. Tallmadge's emotions were indescribable upon reading the letter. In another letter, Tallmadge sheds more light on the situation, explaining that he had been on duty when Major André was brought to the Regiment at North Castle on September 23rd, 1780. He had not returned until the evening and was informed of the capture by Lieutenant Colonel Jameson. Tallmadge was astonished by the decision to send the prisoner to General Arnold at West Point and took immediate measures to reverse this decision. He first requested leave for an official purpose, which he did not disclose, and when this was denied, he arranged for the prisoner's return, which he accomplished by late evening. Tallmadge questioned why Jameson had sent Major André to Arnold, as he had not been present when the decision was made. However, he recalled that Jameson had expressed great confidence in Arnold, which was shared throughout the army. Until the discovery of the papers on Anderson, there had been no suspicion of Arnold's lack of patriotism or political integrity. Tallmadge's acquaintance with Arnold's character dated back to his time at Yale College, where Arnold resided in New Haven. At that time, Tallmadge still thought Arnold was without honor. However, as the Revolutionary War drew near and Arnold showed enthusiasm and bravery in capturing Burgoyne, it appeared that his earlier dishonest behavior had been overlooked. When Arnold was placed in command of West Point, Tallmadge had official communications with him, particularly regarding private correspondence with individuals in New York. When Arnold turned traitor, Tallmadge was initially concerned for his friends in New York, but since he had never revealed their names to Arnold, they remained undiscovered, despite Arnold's efforts to find out. The narrative then delves into the life of Benedict Arnold as observed by members of his military family during July, August, and September 1780, when he commanded the fortifications at West Point. Upon taking command, Arnold invited Colonel Richard Varick to join his military family as an aid and secretary.

Charles Fourier, a French philosopher and social theorist, introduced the concept of "passional attraction" (attraction passionelle) to describe his vision for societal reform. He believed that the existing structure of the world, including its economic, political, and social systems, hindered individuals from pursuing their innate passions, thus preventing the achievement of universal harmony. Fourier maintained that rather than forcing individuals to conform to present societal standards, the existing structures of society ought to be transformed to align with personal passions, since such structures were created by humans and not established by divine will. Fourier proposed a new approach to education and socialization, which he referred to as "social science." By understanding and applying this knowledge, he envisioned the creation of new economic and social formations called "Associations." These Associations would be designed to allow individuals to follow their passions, thereby advancing society towards universal harmony. Fourier was recognized for his methodical way of classifying and enumerating ideas. He identified 12 basic passions of humanity, which he organized into three branches of a "passional tree." The first branch consisted of "luxurious passions," which related to the five senses. The second branch comprised the "affective passions," covering love, friendship, and parenthood. The third branch, frequently neglected, consisted of the "distributive passions," encompassing the drive for political maneuvering, the longing for diversity, and the fervor for religious endeavors. Fourier termed the collective sum of all these passions as "unityism." He characterized unityism as a universal feeling of benevolence, suggesting that by embracing and nurturing these passions, society could achieve a state of harmony and well-being for all its members.

"Gentlemen, I present to you a tall and splendid woman, noble in form, with a commanding nose that exudes majesty. She held a deep affection for me, and her lineage was equally impressive. Her uncle, a law stationer, suffered a financial setback of eight hundred pounds. This brings us to the three distinct types of this honorable profession. In my opinion, their respective ranks have not been accurately determined. Perker has always been admired and respected; Dodson and Fogg have faced universal condemnation; Mr. Pell, however, has remained largely unnoticed. Let us now assess the merits of these three gentlemen fairly. If Perker were alive today, he would likely face trial for his role in the Eatanswill election scandal. What is the real issue with Dodson and Fogg, aside from the Ramsey affair? That incident is merely a tale recounted by the clerk Wicks, whose credibility is questionable. What other actions did Dodson and Fogg take that led to such widespread disapproval? They initiated a lawsuit for breach of promise to marry, a move that some may argue should never be pursued. They also made a minor arrangement regarding costs, which, while unprofessional, does not justify the harsh criticism they have received. As for Mr. Pickwick, he had no complaints about their conduct, and it was quite inappropriate for him to use such language under the circumstances. However, there is nothing to be said against Mr. Pell, except for a slight exaggeration about his friendship with the Lord Chancellor, a desire we all can understand. While I advocate for Mr. Pell to be recognized as the foremost in this matter, I regretfully assign Mr. Perker the third position. Now, let us move on to discuss the counsel mentioned in this remarkable work. Before delving into the more prominent figures, I would like to highlight a lesser-known member of the Bar, Mr. Prosee. Few of you may have heard of him, but he once dined with Mr. Perker at Montague Place, Russell Square. The gathering was rather dull, with attendees including two country agents, Mr. Snicks, the Life Office Secretary, Mr. Prosee, the eminent counsel, three solicitors, a Commissioner of Bankrupts, a special pleader from the Temple, a young man with keen insights on the law of demises, and several other distinguished individuals. I have always associated Mr. Prosee with the Equity Bar, perhaps due to the suggestive nature of his name. Now, let us turn our attention to the more renowned counsel, Serjeant Snubbin. "We've done everything necessary," Mr. Perker stated. "I have retained Serjeant Snubbin." "Is he a capable man?" Mr. Pickwick inquired. "Capable?" Perker replied. "My dear sir, Serjeant Snubbin is at the pinnacle of his profession. He handles three times as much work as any other individual in court and takes part in all cases. However, I must mention that among our profession, we say that Serjeant Snubbin leads the court by the nose." "I would like to meet him," said Mr. Pickwick. "Meet Serjeant Snubbin?" Perker responded in disbelief. "My dear sir, that is impossible! To see Serjeant Snubbin, one must first pay a consultation fee and schedule a meeting. It cannot be done otherwise." Thus, Mr. Pickwick faced the challenge of meeting his own counsel. He could not understand why, following the engagement of a professional and the payment for their services, there would still be any barriers to accessing them. I will not discuss tonight whether or not the legal profession should be divided into two parts, but I do argue that any system that hinders litigants from having full personal communication with those they have paid to represent them is both anomalous and absurd. However, Mr. Pickwick was a determined individual, and he did manage to meet Serjeant Snubbin. He delivered a short address to the learned gentleman that was not only worthy of his attention but also of every member of the Bar, including your humble servant. "Gentlemen of your profession," Mr. Pickwick continued, "you witness the worst aspects of human nature. All its disputes, ill-will, and animosity are laid bare before you. You understand from your experience with juries that much depends on the effect, and you may be inclined to attribute to others a desire to use deception and self-interest, the very tools you employ with pure honesty and the best intentions for your clients. I believe this is the reason for the common, albeit vulgar, perception of lawyers as suspicious, distrustful, and overly cautious. Although there may be a risk in making this statement under these conditions, I have decided to speak out clearly, as my friend Mr. Perker has mentioned, that I am not guilty of the accusations brought against me.

For years, a group of men have defied the island's authorities and terrorized the people living on the plains at the foot of Mount Etna. Currently, they all claim to be republicans, and had it not been for Bixio's arrival, they would have established a reign of terror. We have executed many, and I believe Bixio has also taught them some harsh lessons. Our presence here has successfully curtailed the revolutionaries' operations in the towns and villages on the plain. However, it will take a long time to suppress brigandage, and there is no intention of attempting such a task now. This will be a task that must be undertaken by the government when Italy achieves her freedom and feels capable of addressing these bands that have been a disgrace to our land for years, if not centuries. We are here solely to curb the revolutionary movement, just as Garibaldi curbed the royal movement by sending Farina out of the island. "And where is Bixio?" you ask. "He has been sweeping through the small towns and villages around the foot of the mountains and is expected to arrive at Bronte this afternoon, which has been the headquarters of this revolutionary activity. I anticipate that he will deal sternly with those who have been most active in inciting the people there. Bixio is the right man for this job. He recognizes that a firm lesson produces more influence on individuals such as these Sicilians compared to leniency or spoken warnings. They must be taught that they should not meddle in state affairs. All these matters should be left to their representatives in parliament and the government. The local authorities of these small towns tend to regard themselves as important figures and indulge in discussing public affairs instead of focusing on their primary responsibility, which is to protect the people in their districts from the incursions of bands of brigands. I assume you'll proceed on your journey tomorrow?" "Yes, I'll leave at dawn; it's not a lengthy ride." "I have approximately twenty mounted men here, Percival. I will send four of them with you." "I'm sure that's not necessary," Frank said. "Well, I'm not so sure. I am not aware of any significant groups operating in the plains currently, though several of these factions have split up, particularly those originating from the mainland, and have not yet moved into the mountains. They are committing crimes at isolated houses or on any travelers they encounter. I need not inform you that their hatred for the red shirts is strong, and in revenge for their fellow members who have been shot or executed, they would definitely kill any of us if they had the chance; thus, it would be advisable for you to have four men accompany you. They could just as well be engaged in that activity for all the happening here right now, since it's as uneventful as a quiet garrison town in Northern Italy. How long do you suppose it will be before we join Garibaldi in Messina?" "Not for a while, I think. If he and Medici succeed in defeating Bosco at Milazzo, as I anticipate they will, he will move directly to Messina without delay. However, his message to Bixio was that it will take some time to prepare for the crossing to the mainland, and that until he sends word for the general to join him, he should continue his work of restoring order, reorganizing the municipal authorities, and placing the administration of the towns and villages in the hands of trustworthy individuals, so that there can be no chance of Mazzini's party causing any serious disturbances again after he has left." "I see you still have your arm in a sling?" "Yes; Mantoni told me that it would not be safe to remove it from the splints for another month, but he is hopeful that when I do, I will be able to use it, though I must not exert it too much. Of course, it's an inconvenience, but I have every reason to be grateful, as I was afraid for a while that I might lose it altogether." "It was a heroic act, the defense of that house." "It was fortunate that the shell struck the stairs just when it did, for another minute would have meant the end of the defense and our lives. As it turned out, that explosion saved four of us, since the injured individuals we transported are all making a recovery, and also preserved the lives of five women and eight children, for, despite their anger, the Neapolitans would surely have displayed no greater cruelty there than they did in the other dwellings they stormed. I have been well rewarded, as Garibaldi has made me a captain." Sarto and Maffio returned at that moment, and the three warmly congratulated Frank on his promotion.

The organizational framework of this entity, as detailed in the 1976 Manual del Dirigente (Leader's Handbook), is structured in a pyramid-like and hierarchical manner. At the apex of this structure is the World Command, a position once held by Livraga. The hierarchy moves downward through several levels, such as the Guardian of Seals, Continental Commands, Central Commands, National or Federal Councilors, Unified Zone Commands, and Branch Chiefs. An iconic representation of the organization is the "Golden Ax," awarded to a specific group of members referred to as "hachados" (ax holders). This prestigious honor is exclusive to those deemed elite and is granted or revoked solely by the World Command. The Central Commands are tasked with selecting hachados according to their qualifications, expecting them to lead simple lives and avoid amassing riches beyond what is necessary for sustenance. Hachados are entitled to request retirement under circumstances such as advanced age or health issues, with the organization committed to supporting their well-being in their later years. Upon retiring, a hachado keeps their honors but is required to surrender the Golden Ax. If their status as a hachado is rescinded, the ax is both retrieved and obliterated. The Manual del Dirigente highlights the importance of maintaining the confidentiality of its content, requiring that the information remain secret not just from the public but also from non-directive members of the organization. It also recommends that leaders use caution in sharing Acropolitan ideas, beliefs, and concepts publicly, adapting their communication to align with the audience's inclinations. Additionally, the manual mandates that the majority of the organization's symbols, salutes, and customs be maintained and preserved.

Metafiction is a literary technique that involves self-reference within a work of fiction. It often involves discussions of aesthetic issues and the relationship between the text and external texts or issues. This method appears in different formats, such as indirect metafiction, which gently shapes the reader's understanding of the text, and direct metafiction, which clearly states the fictional character of the work. Metafiction can be further categorized into critical and non-critical forms. Critical metafiction aims to examine the artificial nature or fictional aspects of a text, typically by challenging or critiquing the work itself. This approach is frequently employed in postmodernist fiction. On the other hand, non-critical metafiction does not aim to criticize or undermine the artificiality or fictionality of a text. Instead, it may be used to suggest that the story being read is authentic, a technique often used in realistic fiction. Furthermore, metafiction can be oriented towards the medium or towards the truth or fiction. Media-centred metafiction focuses on the medial quality of fiction or narrative, while truth- or fiction-centred metafiction places additional emphasis on the truthfulness or inventiveness of a text. An example of non-critical, truth-centred metafiction would be the suggestion of a story being authentic, which is a common device in realistic fiction. A prominent instance of metafiction is Miguel de Cervantes' "Don Quixote, Part Two," which was published in 1615. Cervantes wrote this sequel a decade after the original "Don Quixote" was released in 1605. The production of the sequel was partly driven by Cervantes' frustration with a fake Part Two that had been published in 1614, authored by Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda. In Cervantes' authentic Part Two, the text engages in metafictional elements, acknowledging its own status as a work of fiction and the artificiality of the narrative. This self-referential method enriches the narrative with additional layers and intricacy, prompting readers to reflect on the essence of fiction and the act of storytelling.

Pragmatism is a philosophical approach that aims to explore the connection between the knower and the known, instead of concentrating on indissoluble facts. In 1868, Charles Sanders Peirce, a central figure in pragmatism, argued that there is no inherent capacity for intuition or introspection that offers unconditional knowledge. He held that our perception of an inner realm originates from inferred possibilities grounded in external realities. Peirce disputed the conventional philosophical methods of introspection and intuition, which have been employed since the era of René Descartes. He maintained that there is no absolutely initial cognition within any cognitive process; rather, these processes can always be divided into more detailed stages. According to Peirce, introspection does not grant us privileged access to knowledge about the mind. The idea of the self arises from our engagement with the external environment, instead of originating from within as an inherent foundation. Peirce also argued that pragmatism and epistemology could not be based on principles from psychology as a distinct scientific discipline. He thought that our actual beliefs frequently differ from what we ought to believe. In his "Illustrations of the Logic of Science" series, Peirce presented both pragmatism and principles of statistics as integral aspects of the scientific method. This position represents a notable departure from the perspectives of many other pragmatists, who generally support a broader naturalism and psychologism. Richard Rorty, another influential pragmatist, expanded upon Peirce's ideas and other related arguments in his work "Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature." In this text, Rorty criticized the efforts of numerous philosophers of science to delineate the boundaries between different areas of philosophical inquiry.

The concept of the good has been a subject of philosophical inquiry for centuries, with various interpretations across different cultures and time periods. Plato, the ancient Greek philosopher, proposed the existence of an eternal realm of forms or ideas, where the greatest of these ideas is the essence of being, known as "The Good." According to Plato, The Good is a perfect and eternal idea that exists independently of human perception. In this perspective, The Good signifies the proper relationship among all existing things, and it is thought to dwell in the mind of the Divine or within a celestial domain. It encompasses various aspects such as harmony in a just political community, love, friendship, the ordered human soul filled with virtues, and the appropriate relationship with the Divine and Nature. Plato's dialogues frequently emphasize the qualities of a philosopher, or a seeker of wisdom, who strives to comprehend and manifest The Good. The idea of the good is also intimately connected to theistic convictions, in which an individual holds faith in the presence of a Supreme Being or deities, whether singular or multiple. Theists might claim that the universe possesses a purpose and inherent worth as determined by these creators, some aspects of which could lie outside human comprehension. One prominent advocate of this perspective is Thomas Aquinas, a medieval philosopher and theologian, who sought to demonstrate the existence of God and define the appropriate relationship that humans should maintain with the divine first cause. Monotheistic信仰者 may also hold the hope for infinite universal love, which is often referred to as "faith." In many religious doctrines, wisdom is defined as the knowledge and understanding of innate goodness. Moreover, the ideas of innocence, spiritual purity, and salvation are closely linked to the notion of the good. These concepts emphasize the importance of moral and spiritual development in achieving a harmonious relationship with the Divine and the natural world. In conclusion, the notion of the good represents a diverse and intricate concept that has been examined by philosophers, theologians, and adherents throughout various cultures and historical eras. It includes a broad spectrum of values and virtues, such as justice, love, friendship, and spiritual purity, all of which aid in comprehending the final aim and significance of existence.

The economic and political landscape of our world today is a testament to the diverse ways in which historical conditions shape the development of societies. This is apparent not only across various races, peoples, nations, and states, but also within the more specific subdivisions of these groups, including regions within states, social hierarchies, and class structures. These diverse components may be depicted as points along a intricate, gradually changing trajectory or as steps on an extremely extended ladder. The passage of time has not impacted all individuals uniformly, and the mere sequence of generations is not a dependable indicator of advancement or growth. The developments we have seen are varied because the achievements within the same unit of time have been varied. There exists a particular resemblance or parallel in how these developments take place, which may occasionally result in more advanced societies impacting and hastening the advancement of less developed ones. However, it is essential to recognize that progress does not represent an inevitable destiny or a divine decree that dictates the unfolding of human history. Our comprehension of progress is not a static, empirical notion, but rather a situational and constrained perspective. It is not a grand design or plan, but a method of research and conception. This perspective is similar to that of Darwinism, which is also a method rather than a modern reinterpretation of the natural philosophy of the past. The notion that progress is relative and dependent on circumstances was initially presented by Saint Simon, who contested the singular, egalitarian, and uniform perspective of the 18th century, exemplified by individuals such as Condorcet. Saint Simon proposed a more nuanced understanding of progress, one that takes into account the various faculties and aptitudes that substitute and compensate for each other. To truly grasp the reasons behind the relativity of progress, it is necessary to move beyond the belief that natural and immediate causes are the sole obstacles to uniform human development. These natural obstacles, such as racial differences or geographical variations, are either insufficient or problematic in explaining the diverse historical and social conditions that exist within the same geographical area. The historic movement has evolved from a time when natural obstacles were largely overcome or significantly limited, thanks to the creation of an artificial field that allowed for further human development. It is clear, then, that the obstacles to uniform progress must be sought within the intrinsic conditions of the social structure itself. This structure has historically taken the form of political organizations aimed at balancing economic inequalities, resulting in a constantly unstable organization. From the earliest known history, society has been striving to form the state or has already fully constructed it. The state is a manifestation of struggle, both internally and externally, as it is primarily an organ and instrument of a certain part of society against the rest, based on the economic domination of one group over another. This society of antitheses, which forms the state, is characterized by various forms of opposition, such as the city versus the countryside, artisans versus peasants, proletarians versus employers, and capitalists versus laborers. These oppositions inevitably lead to a hierarchy, whether it be a fixed system of privileges, as in the Middle Ages, or a more subtle hierarchy produced by the automatic action of economic competition, as in our time. This economic hierarchy corresponds to what can be described as a hierarchy of souls, intellects, and minds. Culture, frequently regarded as the aggregate of advancement, has remained and persists in being profoundly unevenly dispersed. The majority of people, due to the nature of their occupations, are fragmented and unable to achieve a complete and normal development. The economics of classes and the hierarchy of social positions give rise to the psychology of classes. The relativity of progress is therefore an unavoidable result of class differences, which generate barriers that may result in relative regression, decline, and potentially the collapse of a whole society. The machines that symbolize the triumph of science can, under the conditions of social opposition, become instruments of impoverishment for millions of artisans and peasants. The progress of technology, which fills cities with goods, can make the lives of peasants more miserable and further humble the condition of the urban poor. All scientific advancement so far has contributed to creating a distinct class of scientists, while keeping the masses, bound by their daily labor, progressively removed from cultural engagement. Progress has been and continues to be partial and one-sided. The groups that gain from it refer to it as human progress, whereas confident evolutionists regard it as the advancement of human nature. This partial progress, which has been built on the oppression of one group by another, is founded on the conditions of opposition that have engendered all social distinctions. The relative freedom of the few results in the servitude of the majority, and law has often served as a protector of injustice. In acknowledging this relativity, it becomes evident that progress represents the moral and intellectual summation of all human sufferings and material disparities. To uncover this inevitable relativity, it was necessary for communism, initially an instinctive movement in the hearts of the oppressed, to evolve into a science and a political party.

The Early Helladic period II, which lasted from 2800 to 2200 BC, saw the appearance of notable settlements in Greece. One such settlement, covering an area of 70 to 80 hectares, was home to an estimated 6,000 to 15,000 people, making it one of the largest settlements of the Bronze Age in the region. One prominent settlement from this period was Lerna, situated in the Argolid region. Lerna may have been the most significant and prosperous of the Early Helladic sites. In this settlement, there was a monumental structure, renowned as the House of the Tiles. This "corridor house" was characterized by multiple innovative architectural elements for its era. One such feature was its roof, which was covered with baked tiles, hence the building's name. The House of the Tiles dates back to the Early Helladic II period, around 2500 to 2300 BC. Scholars have proposed various interpretations for the building's purpose. It has been proposed that it could have served as the residence of an influential individual from the community, a precursor to a palace, or an administrative hub. Some have also considered it a communal structure or common property of the townspeople. However, the exact functions of the building remain uncertain due to the lack of small finds that could indicate its specific uses. The House of the Tiles featured a stairway accessing a upper level and was covered by a tiled roof. The debris discovered at the site included thousands of terracotta tiles that had dropped from the roof. While comparable roofs were also identified at the Early Helladic site of Akovitika and subsequently in the Mycenaean settlements of Gla and Midea, they only gained prominence in Greek architecture during the 7th century BC. The walls of the House of the Tiles were built with sun-dried bricks set upon stone bases. This architectural style reflects the innovative building techniques of the time. Though its precise function remains uncertain, the House of the Tiles serves as a symbol of the sophistication and wealth characteristic of the Early Helladic era in Greece.
