The Homeric question refers to an academic debate concerning the authorship of the Homeric epics, specifically the "Iliad" and the "Odyssey," and explores the connection between the name "Homer" and these literary works. This discussion became prominent in the 19th century, acting as a key divergence between two contrasting schools of thought: the Analysts and the Unitarians. The beginnings of the Homeric question date back to the 18th century, a time characterized by a growing fascination with popular ballads and folktales. During this period, scholars started to acknowledge that the Homeric epics were probably passed down orally prior to being recorded in writing. This realization suggested that the texts may have been compiled much later than the traditional dating of "Homer" himself. One prominent participant in this discussion was the Italian philosopher Giambattista Vico, who claimed that the epics were not the work of a single gifted poet but instead represented the cultural output of an entire community. In his 1769 "Essay on the Original Genius and Writings of Homer," Robert Wood contended that Homer was uneducated and that the epics had been passed down through oral tradition. However, Wood's comparison of Homer to the supposed Scottish oral poet Ossian, whose works were published by James Macpherson in 1765, has since been discredited, as Ossian was later revealed to be a fabrication by Macpherson. The German scholar Friedrich August Wolf was instrumental in progressing the Homeric question. In his critique of Emmanuel-Pierre-Louis de Villoison's 1788 edition of the A and B scholia on the "Iliad," Wolf recognized that the scholia offered definitive proof of the oral transmission of the poems. Based on this, Wolf released his "Prolegomena ad Homerum" in 1795, in which he argued that the Homeric poems were created around the middle of the 10th century BCE and were passed down orally prior to being recorded in writing. This work played a major role in shaping the later discussion regarding the Homeric question.

"A Dirge" by James Russell Lowell is a poignant reflection on the life and death of a poet, whose heart has found eternal peace beneath the cold earth. The poet lies buried under the whispering green trees, the soothing buzz of bees, and the sleepy clover. A smooth gurgle of a blue stream murmurs over his grave, as the sun shines down from the blue sky above. Three paces from the silver strand, the poet is gently laid in the fine, white sand, clutching a lily in his hand. His body is not confined by the coarse earth or the gloomy coffin-lid. Instead, sweet birds sing at his sunny burial, and meek forget-me-nots grow where his large, blue eyes once lay hidden beneath the turf. The poet's soul is unbound, his heart brimming with love, truth, forgiveness, and mercy. He resides among enigmas, with traces of calmer heavens reflected in his gaze. His great heart is filled with hope and youth, tiding over the waves of want, woe, and wrong. He strives to win the world with his angelic song, despite the challenges he faces. The poet's transgression is perceiving and listening beyond today's limited horizon, into a reality more genuine and luminous. He longs for the light of the new world, yet he is left heartbroken. His brethren stand in fear, unable to hear the sounds of the land that the poet's quick ear caught long ago. The poet does not desire the poet's wreath, but he secures it too quickly. Beneath it lies scorn, loneliness, and death, gnawing at his brain with burning teeth. He is rich in nobility, his life's essence devoted to blessing, yet he is forced to engage in strife with evil and negotiate with famine and suffering. The poet's spirit soars high above the spheres, seeking its starry peers. It comes not back to face the jeers of brothers who denied it. Star-crowned, the poet possesses the deeps of God, and his white body sleeps where the lone pine forever keeps patient watch beside it. In "Sonnet to My Mother" by T. Holley Chivers, the poet expresses his deep love and gratitude for his mother's unwavering love and care from the moment he was born. His mother's soul dwells in his heart, nurturing him and shaping him into a semblance of herself. The poet acknowledges his mother as his first and last friend, lost in her love. Miss Leslie's "Boston Ramblings" delves into the city's deep devotion to its historical legacy and customs. Bostonians have long cherished the relics and memories of their early settlers and the revolution. However, modern improvements and the pursuit of financial gain are gradually replacing the veneration for the places and things connected with their history. The author observes the vanishing of numerous old-fashioned and possibly unattractive edifices that previously evoked a feeling of poetic beauty, love, and charm. Modern, more lucrative structures have replaced them, leaving just a handful of remnants from the past. The author laments the loss of the "old familiar faces" of these time-honored habitations. Fortunately, Faneuil Hall remains protected by the city's charter, ensuring that it will never be sold or its ground appropriated for any other purpose. The edifice still stands nearly as it was when the walls of its chief apartment echoed with the acclamations of the people discussing the principles that led to their self-emancipation from the sway of oppression.

The figure within the painting is immense, her flowing gown highlighting her imposing stature. She simpers in profile, her elongated chin contrasting with her precariously slanted posture. The lamplight, emanating from below as if she stands on a grand platform, casts peculiar shadows across her expansive face. In the background, the outline of musicians, dressed in black with white shirts, appears against the wall, their shadows blending with posters, guitars, and stained fingerprints. This artwork captures a vivid sense of reality with remarkable breadth and boldness. However, its flaw lies in its unsettling effect on the viewer, which is unfortunate given that the sight of a graceful, passionate dancer is not inherently displeasing. "El Jaleo" leans toward unattractiveness, and aside from the dancer's bulky skirts, it fails to convey a feeling of calm. This is sharply contrasting with the appealing, dark-hued figure in the Tangerine-themed painting shown at the 1880 Salon. This piece, born from the artist's visit to the African coast during his time in Spain, depicts a woman standing on a rug beneath a grand white Moorish arch. Her hands lift her flowing fabric, throwing her head into shadow, with only her painted eyes and eyebrows visible above her wrapped mouth. She looks down at the fumes from a lovely censer or chafing-dish on the floor, her silent reflection and pearl-hued garments beneath the shining plastered arcade both enchanting and distressing the observer. The painting is exquisite, a radiant interplay of whites, a testament to the artist's skill in differentiating similar yet distinct tones. When dividing the accolades Mr. Sargent has garnered for his finest works, it is crucial to recognize the merit of his 1882 painting of four little girls, which was exhibited the following year to much acclaim. The artist has created a vivid, subdued French interior, offering a complete portrayal of a family's playful environment, employing an unusual approach that avoids the conventional symmetric placement of figures. The scene is viewed as a whole, yet the children in their white pinafores (painted with such power and poetry) stand out with a personal life. Two sisters stand hand in hand at the back, accompanied by a pair of towering, ornate jars that seem to share in the life of the painting. The porcelain and the children's aprons gleam together, while a mirror in the background catches the light. Another girl, with abundant hair and slim legs, stands to the left, and the youngest sits on the floor, playing with her doll. The naturalness of the composition, the charm of the overall effect, the light and fluent style, and the presence of hidden insights and innate understanding combine to make this painting a remarkable feat for a young artist at twenty-six. Mr. Sargent is occasionally faulted for lacking "finish," yet if "finish" denotes the highest expression of touch, "The Hall with the Four Children" may function as a lasting example. If the portrait of the Spanish dancer demonstrates the limitations of Impressionist technique, this painting exemplifies the successes it can attain. Like the young lady holding a flower, this piece encourages the viewer to reflect on what still awaits the artist. It raises the question of whether it is advantageous for an artist to master their craft so early in life, potentially leading to a sense of irresponsibility or a lack of reverence. Such reflections belong to those who remain critical even in their most sincere appreciations, doubting that it might be preferable for an artist to struggle with unresolved challenges. When this situation does not arise, the question regarding the artist's future becomes more specific. "What will he do with it?" we inquire, alluding to the artist's refined abilities. It becomes a question of accountability, and we expect the artist to meet a greater standard. This applies to Mr. Sargent; his broad understanding of painting might lead him to manipulate it or perhaps misuse it. Despite having focused mainly on portraits, his willingness to experiment and take risks distinguishes him from those who stick strictly to the literal. Mr. Sargent's work has been predominantly represented by portraits, but there are a few subject-pictures that stand out. A small painting exhibited at the Grosvenor Gallery, for instance, depicts a group of Venetian girls engaged in humble household tasks in the dim hall of an old palazzo. The light filtering through the shutters illuminates the scagliola pavement, and the vegetables they work with are painted with such enchanting detail that they appear as valuable as magnified pearls. The figures are remarkably natural and vivid, and the painter's touch is light and fine, evoking the small, familiar Venetian realities without succumbing to the clichés that often plague depictions of Italy. The National Register of Historic Places serves as a listing that acknowledges historic districts, sites, buildings, and properties within the United States. It relies on the standards of National Historic Landmarks, which also outline exclusions and exceptions to those exclusions. The register functions as a type of official recognition, yet it mainly holds an honorary nature with certain federal financial benefits. Inclusion in the National Register automatically encompasses all National Historic Landmarks, as well as historic areas managed by the National Park Service. This comprises National Historic Sites (NHS), National Historical Parks, National Military Parks/Battlefields, National Memorials, and specific National Monuments. In some instances, historic sites outside the United States that have a connection to the country, such as the American Legation in Tangier, Morocco, are also listed. Listing in the National Register does not impose any restrictions on private property owners concerning the use of their property. However, certain states and municipalities might have legislation that applies once a property is included in the register. When federal funds or a federal permit process is involved, Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966 comes into effect. This section requires the involved federal agency to evaluate the effects of its activities on historic resources. The National Register of Historic Places and its related standards seek to safeguard and maintain the nation's extensive historical legacy, guaranteeing that these important locations are identified and preserved for posterity.

The idea of "creaturely freedom" as it relates to libertarianism is a subject of discussion in both philosophy and theology. Molinists, who support the compatibility of God's all-knowing nature with human free will, acknowledge that beings possess freedom in the libertarian interpretation. However, they argue against the notion that counterfactuals of creaturely freedom lack truth values, as some critics suggest. Some philosophers and theologians who raise the grounding objection suggest that instead of counterfactuals of freedom being definitively true, it is the probable counterfactuals that are actually true. This implies that instead of asserting, "God knows that in situation C, being X will freely act A," it would be more precise to state, "God knows that in situation C, being X would likely act A." Nevertheless, Edward Wierenga has noted that probable counterfactuals are still contingent truths and hence encounter the identical grounding objection. Molinists have offered two main responses to this argument. First, William Lane Craig argues that for a counterfactual of freedom to be true, it is not necessary for the events they refer to actually exist. Instead, it is sufficient that they would exist under the specified conditions. This viewpoint implies that if God were to generate multiple universes across different dimensions, allowing individuals within them libertarian free will, then counterfactuals of freedom might be established through the occurrences in these distinct universes. The second response to the grounding objection involves questioning why God would need to create such universes to know how events would unfold. Critics argue that the very nature of how events would turn out could serve as the grounding for statements about how they would turn out. This approach invites additional debates and challenges in the philosophical and theological conversations regarding divine foreknowledge and human freedom.

Petrofiction, also known as oil fiction, is a literary genre that centers on the significance of petroleum in society and its influence on the human experience. The term was initially coined by Amitav Ghosh in 1992 during his review of Abdul Rahman Munif's novel "Cities of Salt." Ghosh sought to categorize literature focusing on the petroleum industry and its societal effects, especially emphasizing the scarcity of works addressing the "oil encounters" between oil-producing and oil-consuming countries. In 2012, Imre Szeman expanded the definition of petrofiction in an editorial for a special edition of the American Book Review. Szeman proposed that the genre encompasses all works that examine "the important role played by oil in contemporary society." This broader scope allows for a more comprehensive understanding of how oil shapes various aspects of modern life. In the 2000s and 2010s, there was an increase in petrofiction literature, fueled by rising awareness of climate change and the idea of peak oil. Consequently, the term has come to be extensively used in literary criticism for examining fiction that challenges society's dependence on a petroleum-based economy and the culture it generates. While critics originally aimed to find works centered on the oil industry before "Cities of Salt," petrofiction has become more prominent in non-Western literature. This genre provides a distinctive viewpoint on the ways in which engagement with oil relates to other significant matters in the Global South. Some scholars have drawn connections between petrofiction and the emergence of climate fiction, as both genres address the challenges and concerns arising from the Anthropocene era. By examining the effects of human actions on the environment, these literary works prompt readers to consider the importance of sustainable development and environmental responsibility. Notable examples of petrofiction include Abdul Rahman Munif's "Cities of Salt" series, which examines the experiences of individuals impacted by the oil industry within a fictionalized Arabian Peninsula context. Other works in this genre continue to shed light on the complex relationship between society, petroleum, and the environment, fostering a deeper understanding of our world's dependence on oil and its implications for the future.

The shore of the Chesapeake between Cape St. Michael—known by early settlers as the northern headland at the mouth of the Potomac—and the Patuxent, is typically flat, marked by a clear, pebbly beach. This shoreline, spanning about twenty miles, is intersected by a single creek, that of St. Jerome, which flows into the bay some five or six miles north of the Potomac. The beach, occasionally interrupted by small elevations that would not be considered hills elsewhere but are notable in this area, rises just enough to offer a clear view over the expansive waters and to distinguish the inland landscape for mariners navigating up the bay. At certain points, these gentle hills end abruptly at the tide in the form of a cliff, while at others, they form a knoll that slopes down to the beach, covered in grass. This feature can be seen near St. Jerome's, where the slope descends steeply to the tide level, leaving a strip of low ground about fifty paces wide between its base and the ordinary waterline. It was on this flat area that, in ancient times, stood the dwelling of Paul Kelpy the fisherman—a long, low building made of deal boards, constructed in the shape of a warehouse or magazine. A quarter of a mile along the beach, hidden under the brow of the slope and nearly obscured by the natural shrubbery, stood a humble cottage. Its low height allowed a man of average stature to touch the roof eaves while standing at the door. The cottage was small, with only two rooms, the largest of which was no more than ten feet square. It was constructed from hewn logs, and its door, strengthened by thick nails and a sturdy padlock, offered protection against all but the most persistent intruders. A small enclosure surrounded the cottage, providing space for a few common garden plants that were well-tended. A few acres on the higher plain above the bank showed signs of cultivation, and fishing equipment scattered around, along with a skiff on the sand, indicated the livelihood of the cottage's occupant. The day prior to the events of our story, roughly an hour before sunset, a gentle drizzle accompanied by a consistent wind from the northeast created a cool, somber atmosphere over the scene, amplifying the feeling of isolation. A slender column of smoke ascending from the cottage's chimney indicated that someone was living there, as evidenced by the large, cross-facened mastiff-bitch peeking out from beneath the roof, serving as a gloomy protector of this lonely location. The flood tide propelled the waves, which pounded nearly against the cottage's entrance with an unending, grating noise.

Relativism, a philosophical concept that suggests varying perspectives may be equally valid, has been criticized by notable philosophers such as Hilary Putnam and Susan Haack, who consider it to be misguided. John Dewey, in his book "The Quest for Certainty," condemned what he called "the philosophical fallacy." He maintained that philosophers frequently assume categories like the mental and the physical without acknowledging that these are nominal constructs designed to tackle particular problems. This oversight can lead to metaphysical and conceptual confusion. Examples of this fallacy include the "ultimate Being" in Hegelian philosophy, the belief in a "realm of value," and the notion that logic, as an abstraction from concrete thought, is disconnected from the action of concrete thinking. David L. Hildebrand captured the problem, noting that neglecting the particular roles of inquiry has caused both realists and idealists to impose the outcomes of thorough abstraction upon experience. Pragmatists, right from the start, sought to transform philosophy and bring it in line with the scientific approach. They argued that idealist and realist philosophies often portrayed human knowledge as lying outside the reach of scientific inquiry. According to pragmatists, these philosophies frequently depended on either a Kantian phenomenology or theories of knowledge and truth based on correspondence. Pragmatists criticized the former for its a priorism and the latter for its reliance on the concept of correspondence.

The concept of "human wisdom" has been a subject of debate and contemplation throughout history. In 1920, historian J. B. Bury suggested that the final aim of human progress for many is a society in which every member experiences complete happiness. However, he also acknowledged that it is impossible to prove whether humanity's unknown destination is indeed desirable. The idea of progress, Bury argued, is akin to concepts like Providence or personal immortality—it can be seen as either true or false, and its validity cannot be definitively proven or disproven. Belief in progress, therefore, is ultimately a matter of faith. In the 1980s, postmodernist thought began to challenge the grand claims made by modernizers. This movement cast doubt on the concept of social advancement, examining the deeds and ideals of radical modernizers such as Joseph Stalin and Mao Zedong, who are typically regarded as authoritarian leaders with an inaccurate perception of progress. Postmodernists contend that the ideas of progress from the 19th and 20th centuries, whether under capitalism or Marxism, are defective. They believe that these ideologies place too much emphasis on technological advancements and material wealth, neglecting the importance of inner happiness and mental peace. According to postmodernist thought, the concepts of dystopia and utopia are essentially the same, representing overarching grand narratives with unattainable conclusions. In summary, the idea of progress has been a topic of ongoing discussion and debate. While some regard it as an essential and beneficial component of human advancement, others cast doubt on its legitimacy and consequences. The postmodernist viewpoint provides a critical analysis of conventional ideas about progress, advocating for a reassessment of what genuinely represents societal development.

The narrative surrounding Daniel Home and his supposed supernatural abilities has been a subject of intrigue and skepticism for many years. It is said that Home possessed an extraordinary power that allowed him to transfer this energy to others, a claim that has been met with both fascination and disbelief. However, a more practical viewpoint proposes that the occurrences linked to Home can be accounted for by more ordinary explanations. Take, for instance, the incident involving a live coal. While some might contend that Home's capacity to manage a burning coal without harm demonstrates his superhuman abilities, a more reasonable explanation can be found in the characteristics of the coal itself. It is quite common for specific sections of coal to be less reactive, or "dead," enabling secure manipulation. Furthermore, the description of Mr. Hall's white hair appearing "silvery" against the coal suggests that the coal was not glowing, indicating that it was likely not as hot as one might assume. The involvement of Sir William Crookes, a renowned scientist, adds a layer of credibility to these events. However, it is important to remember that even the most learned individuals can be deceived. Crookes' account of witnessing Home placing his hands in the fire lacks the precision and detail one would expect from a scientific observer. His account of Home working with a "bright red" coal is also doubtful, since it fails to consider that the coal might not have been evenly heated. The narrative then shifts to the subject of musical phenomena, with Home once again at the center of the discussion. His alleged ability to induce spirits to play an accordion while he held it is a fascinating claim, but one that is easily explained through sleight of hand and deception. The circumstances in which these performances occurred—typically in low light and from behind a curtain—offer considerable chances for deception. The use of a cage to contain the accordion during a séance led by Sir W. Crookes presents a more challenging scenario. However, the absence of any witness to the keys moving during the performance raises questions about the authenticity of the event. The possibility of a hidden musical box or the use of hooks and loops to manipulate the accordion cannot be discounted. The account of Mrs. Annie Eva Fay, another medium who asserted she communicated with spirits via music, additionally demonstrates the possibility of deceit in such presentations. Her séances, which involved her sitting in a circle with a bell and a guitar, were designed to create the illusion of supernatural activity. The incorporation of darkness along with her husband, "Colonel" Fay, within the circle implies that the pair could have been collaborating to produce the semblance of ghostly musicians. The discovery that Mrs. Fay's performances might be recreated using straightforward techniques, including tape manipulation and concealed items, raises questions about the validity of her assertions. The fact that she offered to reveal her secrets for a fee further undermines her credibility. In conclusion, while the stories of Daniel Home and other mediums may be captivating, it is essential to approach these accounts with a critical eye. The use of deception, sleight of hand, and the manipulation of the senses are common tools employed by those seeking to create the illusion of supernatural phenomena. As with any historical account, it is crucial to consider the context, the motivations of the individuals involved, and the possibility of alternative explanations before accepting these tales as evidence of the paranormal.

As the solemn silence was broken by the declaration "Condemned to death," a collective murmur of compassion rippled through the crowd. This was followed by a hushed silence as the rest of the document was read out. Another murmur arose upon hearing the sentences: Maroncelli to hard imprisonment for twenty years, and Pellico for fifteen. The Captain signaled for us to descend, and we cast one last glance around before returning to the court-yard. We ascended the grand staircase and were led back to the room from which we had been taken. The manacles were removed, and we were soon escorted back to San Michele. CHAPTER LIV The prisoners who had been sentenced before us had already departed for Lubiana and Spielberg, accompanied by a police commissary. He was now expected to return and guide us to our destination. However, a month passed before he arrived. To distract myself, I spent my time conversing and listening to others, including Maroncelli, who read me some of his literary works, and I reciprocated by sharing my own. One evening, I read my play "Ester d’Engaddi" from the window to Canova, Rezia, and Armari, and the following night, "Iginia d’Asti." However, at night, I became restless and miserable, struggling to sleep. I was both eager and apprehensive to learn how my family had received the news of my misfortune. Eventually, I received a letter from my father, which revealed that my last letter to him had not been sent as I had requested from the Inquisitor. This caused me great distress, as my father had been under the impression that I would be released, only to read the dreadful sentence in the Milan Gazette. I could not express the contempt and anger I felt upon learning that my letter had been withheld, and I deeply empathized with the suffering of my family. Although I now believe there was no malice in this delay, I still view it as a cruel act, an eager, infernal desire to cause my loved ones immense pain. I was further enraged to learn that my companions were planning to celebrate Easter week before their departure. As for me, I could not understand the concept of forgiveness, and the notion of taking part in such a celebration appeared unthinkable. CHAPTER LV Finally, the German commissioner arrived and informed us that we would be departing within two days. He also provided some reassuring information: after returning from Spielberg, he had met with the Emperor in Vienna, who told him that our punishment would not extend for twenty-four hours, but only twelve. This was meant to signify that the pain would be divided, or half the punishment remitted. Although this information was not officially communicated to us, there was no reason to doubt the commissioner's words, especially since he was open about it and it was known to the entire commission. However, I could not find solace in this news. To me, seven and a half years in chains and solitude seemed no different from fifteen; I believed it would be impossible to survive such a long period. My health had worsened, marked by intense chest pain and a constant cough, causing me to worry that my lungs might be compromised. I ate little and struggled to digest what I consumed. Our departure took place on the night of March 25th. We were allowed to bid farewell to our friend, Cesare Armari. A sbirro chained us in a transverse manner, linking the right hand to the left foot, making escape impossible. We boarded a gondola, with the guards rowing us towards Fusina. Upon arrival, we found two boats prepared for us. Rezia and Canova were placed in one, while Maroncelli and I were in the other. The commissary took charge of two prisoners, and an under-commissary was responsible for the remaining ones. Six or seven armed police guards completed our convoy, some in the boats and others in the Vetturino's box. Being compelled to depart one's homeland owing to adversity is invariably distressing, yet to be uprooted under duress, banished to an unforgiving environment, and subjected to isolation within grim cells for days, hours, or even years, constitutes a calamity so abysmal that language fails to encapsulate its entire dread. Before we crossed the Alps, I realized how much my country meant to me. The sympathy we received from people of all ranks was an irresistible appeal to my affection and gratitude. In every city, village, and even the humblest of dwellings, news of our conviction had spread, and we were anticipated. In various locations, the commissioners and guards struggled to disperse the crowds that had gathered around us. It was notable to observe the kind and compassionate sentiments shown in our favor. In Udine, we experienced a touching incident. Upon arriving at the inn, the commissary ordered the courtyard door to be closed to keep the people at bay.

Eschenbach's "Parzival," the Ethiopian national epic "Kebra Nagast," the tales of Prester John, and the imagery of Chartres Cathedral are some of the historical and mythological sources examined in the book. The author, Graham Hancock, posits that the Knights Templar sought the lost Ark of the Covenant and other relics at the Temple Mount in Jerusalem during the 12th century. It is suggested that an Ethiopian king in exile, possibly Lalibela, made contact with the Knights Templar while residing in Jerusalem during that time. This hypothesis is supported by the architectural legacy of Lalibela, particularly the Church of Saint George, which is intriguing in the context of Gothic architecture's development. The Ethiopian Church, concerned about the potential loss of the Ark to the Knights Templar, allegedly dispatched emissaries to Pope Clement V in 1306. The book argues that the Catholic Church's apprehension regarding the Knights Templar gaining the Ark's power was a contributing factor in Pope Clement V's decision to initiate the prosecution and arrest of the Knights Templar in 1307. The book achieved commercial success but was met with unfavorable reviews from critics. Jonathan Kirsch from the Los Angeles Times referred to it as a mix of travel writing, genuine adventure, and a mystery thriller, yet mainly labeled it as amateurish scholarship paired with a creative storyline, similar to sharing ghost tales by a campfire. Desmond Ryan of the Philadelphia Inquirer humorously questioned the extent of the author's speculation.

Noir fiction, a genre characterized by its dark, moody atmosphere and morally complex characters, has a rich history that spans several decades and continents. Pioneered by American authors such as Elliott Chaze, Charles Williams, Gil Brewer, Harry Whittington, Peter Rabe, and Lionel White, alongside David Goodis and Jim Thompson, this literary movement has evolved and expanded over time. In the 1980s, Black Lizard, an American publisher, played a significant role in reviving interest in noir fiction by re-releasing many classic works. Today, Akashic Books continues to celebrate the genre with a diverse collection of noir short-story anthologies. The noir genre has also found a strong foothold in Europe, with notable authors such as Jean-Claude Izzo and Massimo Carlotto contributing to its growth. According to Italian publisher Sandro Ferri, "Mediterranean noir" stands out for its exploration of the dual nature of Mediterranean life. These novels frequently portray Mediterranean cities as areas tainted by crime, yet retaining an enchanting allure. The genre is characterized by a dual nature, contrasting the Mediterranean way of life centered on exquisite wine, cuisine, camaraderie, and sociability against the grim aspects of violence, corruption, greed, and misuse of power. James Ellroy stands out as a notable figure among modern writers who employ both hardboiled and noir styles. He characterizes noir as "the most scrutinized branch of the hard-boiled school of fiction," and emphasizes its attraction through the "thrill of moral surrender and the surrender to sensuality." Ellroy also recognizes the societal relevance of noir, pointing out its focus on major topics like race, class, gender, and systemic concerns. Noir fiction maintains its lasting appeal due to its capacity to explore the intricacies of human nature and society, providing readers with an engaging and intellectually stimulating encounter.

Horace Townsend, known affectionately as "H. T.," emerged from a perilous ordeal with a renewed vigor, his cheeks flushed with warmth and his body imbued with a newfound strength. He rose, without shoes and wearing only his shirt-sleeves, his hair stuck to his forehead and his garments tight against his skin, an inconspicuous presence yet one that would command the respect of any painter—a man who had recently overcome a formidable peril through selfless kindness. Margaret Hayley, noting his tall and upright stance, perceived not the faintest suggestion of anything lacking in romance. Perhaps in her view, his dark skin appeared to emit a sort of holy glow, a symbol of her admiration, a sharp contrast to the emotions she had recently had to convey. It was only such an intense regard that could account for her later behavior, which, given a woman of her great self-respect, caused a severe inner struggle that made any misfortune that might have happened in the Pool's water appear like a blessing by contrast. Halstead Rowan, assured by his admiration for his new friend's conduct and not eager to express it hastily, had performed what his wounded hand permitted—jumping across the stream to recover the discarded shoes and coat from the rock where they rested. While the rest of the group, with the exception of the distraught Mrs. Brooks Cunninghame, who was still tending to her barely revived son, gathered around the new hero to offer their thanks and congratulations, it was Margaret Hayley who took his hand. Ignoring the disapproving scowl of Captain Hector Coles, she said, "I do not know, sir, by what name to thank you—" "I believe I am right in calling you Miss Hayley," he replied, his voice still somewhat weak and tremulous. "His name is Horace Townsend, and he is a lawyer from Cincinnati." Thus, the mystery of the initials was resolved, and we can now refer to him by his full name, as those who had noticed the initials but not taken the trouble to learn his full name from the arrival book at the office had done. "I was only partly deliberately the cause of your perilous predicament, Mr. Townsend," Margaret continued, "and yet I cannot regret the freedom I exercised, for it may have saved a life that would have been lost, and allowed me to observe an act of selfless kindness that I will never forget, nor cease to admire for as long as I live." "You do me too much honor," he responded, his voice now a bit steadier. I have merely revealed my own vulnerability. There was no danger to me in the water, as I am a capable swimmer and should be able to dive well. However, I must have stayed under too long, for I could not find the child immediately, and the cold water undoubtedly affected me after getting warm from climbing over the logs. That is all, and I sincerely hope we can all put this disagreeable event behind us, as I definitely will once I manage to locate some dry garments." He spoke in a pleasant manner, though lacking the carefree optimism that defined his rival of the day—the hero of the bear-stakes. As he finished speaking, he bowed and turned away, suggesting that the conversation had reached its conclusion. Margaret Hayley also moved away and rejoined her escort. Halstead Rowan approached with the coat and shoes, and as he placed them on the rock at Townsend's feet, he grasped his hand with his unwounded one, conveying a deep sense of respect and admiration. "I am nowhere!" he cried. I confronted you about that log, yet you ventured into places I wouldn't care to tread, pursuing a noble cause, whereas mine was just a trick. And by the way—" They were now a little apart from the others, and Rowan spoke in a low voice, "do you know where your head lay when you came to?" "Hush! For heaven's sake, hush!" Townsend replied urgently, his look causing Rowan to stop the conversation right away. The company soon began to ascend the steps, carrying the revived boy and accompanying his mother. Townsend successfully slipped the discarded shoes over his damp stockings, fastened his coat, and joined the rear-guard with little help. Despite the discomfort of his continued dampness, he was undoubtedly consoled by the thought that he had survived a plunge into the Pool where few men had ventured and emerged alive, and perhaps even more so by other, more complex reflections. An hour later, the entire group had returned to the Profile House, where Horace Townsend, now known by his full name, enjoyed a dry change of clothes, a slight headache, and a nap that left him refreshed as if he had bathed in the Pool for health reasons.

"Extending MARC for Subject Access," edited by Toni Petersen and Pat Molholt, is a publication by G.K. Hall that delves into the use of MARC (Machine-Readable Cataloging) for subject access in libraries. The book includes several papers on visual resources, such as "Access to Diverse Collections in University Settings: the Berkeley Dilemma" by Howard Besser and Maryly Snow, and "Visual Depictions and the Use of MARC: A View from the Trenches of Slide Librarianship" by Maryly Snow, both published in 1990. In 1991, Tim Berners-Lee began working on a hypertext graphical-user-interface (GUI) and coined the term "World Wide Web" for his program. That same year, "Facilities Standards for Art Libraries and Visual Resources Collections," edited by Betty Jo Irvine, was published by Libraries Unlimited for ARLIS/NA. Additionally, "World Architecture Index: a Guide to Illustrations," compiled by Edward H. Teague, was released by Greenwood Press as part of its Art Reference Collection No. 12. The Visual Resources Association (VRA) established its listserv, VRA-L, in 1992, providing a crucial communication tool for its members who are visual resources curators. In 1993, Oxford University Press published the "Users' Guide to The Art and Architecture Thesaurus" alongside the electronic edition. The VRA formed its Data Standards Committee in March 1994. In September of that same year, Marc Andreessen departed from the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) to found Mosaic Communications Corp, which would eventually evolve into Netscape. Mosaic's launch marked the beginning of the World Wide Web for the general public. In 1994, the initial image database, SPIRO, was introduced on the World Wide Web. In 1995, the "Concordance of Ancient Site Names" was edited and published, further contributing to the growing body of work on visual resources and subject access in libraries.

The remarkable story of carrier pigeons, a breed with an innate ability to return home from great distances, has fascinated societies for centuries. They have been subjected to trials involving travel across vast oceanic distances, yet consistently navigate their way home with precise determination. This distinctive characteristic has proved highly beneficial in numerous human activities, especially in warfare, where they have served to convey messages through enemy territory. A notable instance involved the German Emperor, who, curious about their reliability, sent a batch of these pigeons from England to Germany. Released from Dover, they all made their way back to Düsseldorf within six hours, an occurrence that generated curiosity and worry among the English, ultimately resulting in a debate in the House of Commons. In a remarkable find, a stone from Mexico's Magdalena district, located in the state of Sonora, was discovered bearing symbols remarkably akin to Chinese writing. A well-educated Chinese individual confirmed the inscription to be authentic, dating back two thousand years and suggesting a Chinese settlement in the region. This contradicts the commonly held belief that Columbus was the first to discover the American continent, implying that Chinese explorers may have reached the area much earlier. Archaeological findings indicate that Chinese expeditions during the early stages of their civilization have also been identified in the Pacific Islands and Australia. King Menelik of Abyssinia's decision to appoint a Russian General as Governor-General over regions near the equator demonstrates his intention to introduce civilization to his people. M. M. de Leontieff, who had earlier traveled to Abyssinia and carried presents from the Czar, is anticipated to have a beneficial impact on the country's progress, similar to how General Gordon contributed in Egypt. The text highlights the unity of humankind, implying that distinctions between different countries are negligible, much like the varied abilities present in one household. It illustrates how environmental factors, such as climate and lifestyle, can significantly influence the physical characteristics of a population over time, as seen in the descendants of light-complexioned individuals living in tropical regions. The author posits that the human races have evolved through detachments from the original human family, each developing unique traits under local influences over thousands of years. The search for knowledge regarding the histories and beginnings of different countries is compared to finding distant relatives, encouraging interest in their paths and the causes behind their divergence from their ancestors. The author recognizes the constraints of written documentation, which dates back only a handful of centuries, and emphasizes the value of alternative historical sources, including carvings on structures and edifices. However, the narrative also acknowledges the vast expanse of time before any form of writing existed, leaving the stories of early humans to be pieced together from fragments and interpretations.

Postmodernism is a complex and multifaceted cultural and intellectual movement that emerged in the mid-20th century. It is characterized by skepticism, relativism, and a general distrust of grand theories and ideologies. Postmodernism has had a significant impact on various fields, including music, art, literature, and philosophy. In the realm of music, postmodernism has manifested in diverse and innovative ways. Jonathan Kramer, a scholar on the subject, has observed that avant-garde compositions, which may be considered modernist by some, often challenge and extend the traditional boundaries of what constitutes music. These compositions can be provocative and unsettling, pushing the listener to reconsider their understanding of the art form. In the 1960s, a group of composers such as Terry Riley, Henryk Górecki, Bradley Joseph, John Adams, Steve Reich, Philip Glass, Michael Nyman, and Lou Harrison aimed to distance themselves from the perceived elitism and dissonance associated with atonal academic modernism. They created music with simpler textures and more consonant harmonies, offering a fresh perspective on musical expression. Concurrently, artists like John Cage questioned the established notions of beauty and objectivity that were prevalent in modernism. Cage's work often incorporated unconventional sounds and methods, further expanding the definition of music. Alongside these advancements in classical and avant-garde music, postmodernism has also impacted popular music genres. Dominic Strinati, an author on postmodernism, highlights the significance of "art rock" and the blending of styles seen in the works of groups like Talking Heads and performers such as Laurie Anderson. The Pet Shop Boys' self-conscious reinvention of disco is another example of postmodern musical innovation. In the late 20th century, American pop star Madonna was identified by avant-garde academics as the "embodiment of postmodernism." Both Christian author Graham Cray and literary scholar Olivier Sécardin argued that Madonna represents postmodernism, whereas Martin Amis referred to her as "possibly the most postmodern figure on Earth." Her constant transformation in appearance and fashion, along with her talent for self-reinvention, has positioned her as an icon of the postmodern period. In the field of philosophy, postmodernism arose during the 1970s as a varied and multifaceted group of scholars started to challenge and examine the prevailing narratives and beliefs of their era. These philosophers often rejected the idea of objective truth and universal values, instead advocating for a more nuanced and context-dependent understanding of knowledge and reality. Overall, postmodernism has had a profound impact on various aspects of culture and society, challenging traditional norms and encouraging a more open and questioning approach to art, music, and thought.

Hildebrand Gurlitt was a well-known German art dealer in the period of the Nazi regime. Between 1939 and 1944, he acquired numerous artworks, excluding those for his personal collection. From these acquisitions, 168 items were designated for the Führermuseum, a museum intended to reflect Adolf Hitler's conception of German art. Gurlitt took advantage of his officially authorized purchasing expeditions to Paris, a city filled with artworks of dubious origin, some of which have since been identified as stolen. These journeys enabled him to increase his personal collection of art and accumulate significant wealth through commissions based on the large amounts paid by the Nazi regime for art purchases. Besides his official responsibilities, Gurlitt also acquired paintings personally, especially from artists targeted by the Nazis. One notable artist was Max Beckmann, who had been in exile in the Netherlands by 1944. In September 1944, Gurlitt and his associate, Erhard Göpel, the local buyer for Hitler's Führermuseum, purchased five pieces from Beckmann. One of the paintings acquired was "Bar, Brown," which Gurlitt kept for personal use. After Gurlitt's passing, his wife put the painting up for sale, but it did not sell. Later, his son Cornelius sold the painting at an auction held by Ketterer in Stuttgart in 1972, where it sold for DM 90,000 after deducting the auctioneer's fees. The identical artwork was subsequently put up for sale at Sotheby's in London and achieved £1.2 million. Beckmann's family accepted the allocation of the sale earnings without objection, viewing Gurlitt's initial acquisition as valid, even though it occurred amidst the difficult situations the artist endured. After the war, Gurlitt was captured along with his wife.

Conrad Martens (1801–1878) was a professional painter who practiced from 1835 until 1878, mainly renowned for his landscape works. His artwork is recognized for its capacity to temper the landscape in accordance with European tastes. Martens' watercolor studies of Sydney Harbour are widely appreciated, as they incorporated Romantic principles into his paintings. He is also noted for joining the scientist Charles Darwin on the HMS Beagle, a voyage that was also made by Augustus Earle. During the period from 1851 to 1885, the Victorian gold rush resulted in a notable surge in settlers and a rise in wealth. The artist S. T. Gill (1818–1880) recorded life on the Australian goldfields, reflecting the spirit of the time. However, the colonial art market during that period showed greater interest in landscape paintings. These were frequently ordered by affluent landowners or traders aiming to display their wealth. One significant landscape painting from that era is "Flood in the Darling" by William Piguenit (1836–1914), which was purchased by the National Gallery of New South Wales in 1895. Other notable artists from that period were Eugene von Guerard, Nicholas Chevalier, William Strutt, John Skinner Prout, and Knud Bull. Louis Buvelot played an important role in landscape painting during the later period. Influenced by the Barbizon school painters, Buvelot embraced a plein air method, characterized by painting outdoors to record the natural light and atmosphere. His work frequently conveyed a more domestic and tranquil perspective of the land, differing from the prior focus on unfamiliarity or peril in Australian landscape art. Buvelot's method, along with his significant impact as a teacher, has prompted some to call him the "Father of Australian landscape painting."

Otto Grashof was a German painter, illustrator, and portraitist known for his distinctive artistic contributions. Thomas Somerscales was an English seascape painter, renowned for his work such as "The Naval Battle of Iquique." In addition to these notable figures, there were several lesser-known painters of the same period whose works, though not widely celebrated, are significant. These include John Searle, María Graham, Johan Heinrich Jenny, Francis Martín Drexel, Camilo Domeniconi, Augusto Borget, Procesa del Carmen Sarmiento, Juan Bianchi, Clara Filleul, Alexander Simón, Giovatto Molinelli, and Theodor Ohlsen. The Chilean Precursors of Chilean painting were a group of artists who, similar to their foreign contemporaries based in Chile, were influenced by European art. These Chilean painters did not follow a unified style but operated concurrently and were instrumental in initiating a new phase of Chilean art through the founding of the Chilean Academy of Painting. Galaz and Ivaelic observed that the works of these artists were deeply linked to the Chilean landscape, its people, and cultural aspects. Among the Chilean painters who were part of this movement, Manuel Antonio Caro stands out as the most remarkable artist of this period. His style was realistic, often depicting customs and folkloric scenes. Some of his renowned works feature "La Zamacueca" and "The Abdication of O’Higgins," and Caro joined the recently established academy. Francisco Javier Mandiola was another notable individual in this movement, recognized for depicting local traditions and regarded as the most gifted student of Raymond. His contributions enriched the vibrant artistic landscape of Chile during that time, highlighting the varied cultural and societal elements of the nation.

In his essay about gardening, Horace Walpole discusses a notion that represents a key principle: the contemporary approach to gardening originated from Bridgeman's invention of the "ha-ha," who was a leading figure in landscape gardening. The "ha-ha" allowed a garden to blend harmoniously with the surrounding countryside, separated only by an invisible barrier rather than a wall. This concept challenges the notion that a garden lover would prefer nature to art, as a garden is, in essence, an artistic creation that replaces the untamed wilderness. The affection for nature, as demonstrated by later individuals such as Lord Byron, may at times approach misanthropy, valuing the wild for its intrinsic worth. However, the landscape gardener believes that their art should be subordinate to nature, incorporating the wider scenery into their designs rather than excluding it. This viewpoint echoes the beliefs of Telford, who considered rivers to exist for the benefit of canals, and Gilpin, who assessed nature through the lens of the "theory of the picturesque." Gilpin observed that although nature's arrangements might appear cold and individualistic, they do not fall into "mannerism." Put differently, nature functions as a sublime landscape artist whose creations must be acknowledged and integrated by the human gardener. An intriguing illustration of this theory appears in a lecture given by Henry Tilney in Jane Austen's "Mansfield Park." Under Walpole's theory, the emergence of the "ha-ha" signifies an increasing partnership between humanity and nature, the landowner and the rural landscape. This alliance is characterized by improved roads and inns, the gradual integration of urban and rural areas, and a growing awareness of the drawbacks of overpopulated cities. The affection for nature has strong foundations, as poets from Chaucer onward have praised the attractiveness of landscapes, the coming of spring, and the magnificence of storms and sunsets. The apathy toward nature shown by the Pope school was a fleeting occurrence, illustrating the confidence of the city dwellers and their contempt for the rural environment. However, the squire class maintained a strong affection for field sports, and as they became influenced by urban intellectuals, they began to express feelings that were clearly depicted in works such as Izaak Walton's "The Compleat Angler." The older poets frequently used nature as a setting for human activities, emphasizing specific events and the pleasures of outdoor pursuits or country pastimes. They adhered to old conventions and engaged in conversations with imaginary shepherds, Robin Hood, or allegorical knights in romantic forests. In contrast, during Pope's time, nature emerged as an abstract or metaphysical deity that could be worshipped with a distinct appreciation. Pope himself, influenced by Bolingbroke and Shaftesbury, expounded on the stars and the animal world in his "Essay on Man." Shaftesbury, in particular, emphasized the aesthetic perspective of nature, asserting that the Good, the True, and the Beautiful are all one, and that the universe impresses us as an artistic embodiment of harmony. This perspective led to a legitimate development of the love for beauty, as seen in works like Akenside's "The Pleasures of Imagination" and Henry Brooke's "Universal Beauty." James Thomson's "The Seasons," with its fine "Hymn of Nature," represents this current of sentiment. Thomson's descriptions of nature, intended to serve as a sermon, show a growing interest in country life and a challenge to the supremacy of the urban wit. However, Thomson's philosophy and observation remain somewhat separate, and his masterpiece, the didactic poem on "Liberty," remains largely forgotten. In summary, the affection for nature has developed through time, shifting from serving as a setting for human activities to being esteemed and revered as an entity in its own right. The landscape gardener's approach to subordinating art to nature and incorporating the wider scenery into their designs reflects a growing appreciation for the beauty and harmony of the natural world.

He was a jay, indeed, and I had just witnessed his rather cad-like behavior towards Mrs. Bevidge," one character remarked. "Then I'm at a loss as to why you were in his company," another responded. "Oh, you do understand, Alan. You mustn't apply logic here! It's like questioning how you became more serious than sober." The brother laughed, unable to argue. "It was the excitement," he explained. "But you can't indulge in such behavior, Bess," he chided, his tone heavy with the weight of his own past mistakes. "I know I shouldn't, but I do," she retorted. "I understand it's detrimental to me, if not to others. Let's make a pact to stop!" "I'm always ready to make such a promise," the young man agreed, his voice tinged with melancholy. He added, "But you have a sharp mind, Bess, and I dislike seeing you act foolishly." "Do you truly, Alan?" the girl inquired, seemingly pleased by his criticism as much as his compliment. "Do you think I have a sharp mind?" "You're the only girl who does," he affirmed. "Oh, I didn't mean to ask for that much! But why can't I utilize it effectively? Other girls draw, play music, write. I only seek the excitement that's bad for me. I wish you could explain it." Alan Lynde did not attempt to answer. The question seemed to redirect his thoughts inward, causing him to feel disheartened. "I possess a sharp mind too, I believe," he began. "Lots of them!" his sister interjected, generously. "There's no man who can compare to you. If I had the chance to converse with you constantly, I would not require the presence of jays. I'm not flattering you. You're always a feast of reason; I have no interest in emotional outpourings. You always take the right view of things when you're being yourself, and even when you're not, you're not stupid. You could be anything you chose." "The problem is that I can't choose," he replied. "Yes, I suppose that is the problem," she agreed. "You shouldn't use such language, Bess," her brother admonished, sternly. "Oh, I don't with everyone," she defended herself. "Never with ladies!" He glanced at her with a smile that was both rueful and humorous. "You got me, I guess," he admitted. "'Touché,' Mr. Durgin says. He fences and speaks French. It's as if an animal were speaking French; you're always anticipating them to speak English. But I don't mind your swearing in my presence; I know it helps to dissipate the tension." She laughed, and coaxed a laugh from him as well. "Is there anything to him?" he asked, once their laughter subsided. "Yes, quite a bit," Bessie replied thoughtfully, and then she went on to recount all that Jeff had told her about himself, describing his composure in dealing with the benevolent Mrs. Bevidge, as she referred to her, and sketching his character as she perceived it. Her sketch was filled with astute conjectures and she made it entertaining for her brother, who, from his own perspective of mischief, undoubtedly judged the original more intelligently. "Well, you'd better avoid him after this," he advised at the end. "Yes," she agreed pensively. "I suppose it's like developing a taste for a very common type of whiskey, isn't it? I see what you mean. If one must indulge, it should be in champagne." She turned to him with a look of keen yet limited understanding, which always makes women's conjectures about vice so amusing or so touching to men. "Better avoid the champagne as well," her brother suggested darkly. "Yes, I know," she conceded, sinking back into her chair and staring dreamily at the fire. After a while, she asked abruptly, "Will you stop if I will?" "I'm afraid I couldn't," he replied. "You could try," she encouraged. "Oh, I'm used to it," he said. "Then it's a deal," she announced, leaping from her chair and moving toward him. She smoothed his hair over his forehead and kissed the spot she had smoothed, despite its unpleasant dampness to her lips. "Poor boy, poor boy! Now, remember! No more jays for me, and no more sprees for you. Jeff Durgin was unsure if Miss Bessie Lynde planned to join Mrs. Bevidge's Thursday gatherings or not.
